claim: About 60% of emerging infectious diseases in humans are of zoonotic origin.
source: About 60% of emerging infectious diseases in humans are of zoonotic origin.
evidence: This is a well-established statistic in the field of emerging infectious diseases, supported by multiple studies cited in the introduction.

claim: 1230 blood-engorged flies were caught in the forests of Gabon.
source: Here, we investigated whether blood meals from hematophagous flies could be used to identify the infectious agents circulating in wild vertebrates. To this aim, 1230 blood-engorged flies were caught in the forests of Gabon.

claim: 30% of blood meals were successfully identified.

claim: The appearance of new pathogens has gradually increased since 1980.

claim: Seven new pathogens appear every year today.
source: Today, seven new pathogens appear every year and this number should reach 15–20 by 2020 (Woolhouse et al., 2008), mostly due to the growth of human activities that increase contact with novel sources of pathogens and favor their spread worldwide (Murray et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Woolhouse et al., 2008.

claim: The number of new pathogens should reach 15-20 by 2020.

claim: The blood meal from unknown host N°110 could have originated from a Kinixys turtle (Kinixys sp.).
source: For example, the blood meal from unknown host N°110 could have originated from a Kinixys turtle (Kinixys sp.).
evidence: This is an inference based on the detected parasite and its known host range.

claim: The blood meals from the unknown hosts N°649, 520, 665, 512 and 819 could have originated from humans (Homo sapiens).
source: Similarly, the blood meals from the unknown hosts N°649, 520, 665, 512 and 819 could have originated from humans (Homo sapiens).
evidence: This is an inference based on the detected parasites and their known host range.

claim: The present study demonstrates the possibility to use hematophagous flies as 'flying syringes' to analyze the diversity of pathogens circulating in wildlife.
source: The present study demonstrates the possibility to use hematophagous flies as 'flying syringes' to analyze the diversity of pathogens circulating in wildlife.
evidence: This is the primary conclusion of the study based on all the data collected.

claim: The use of PCR systems targeting fragments of shorter size could potentially improve the performance of detection.
source: We think that there is now room for improvement of the tool; for instance, by improving the methods used to identify the blood meals and the pathogens. Since DNA is likely to be degraded in many blood meals (Calvignac-Spencer et al., 2013; Schnell et al., 2012), the use of PCR systems targeting fragments of shorter size could potentially improve the performance of detection.
evidence: This is a speculation about how to improve the method, supported by citations to Calvignac-Spencer et al., 2013 and Schnell et al., 2012.

claim: A trial study using a PCR system amplifying a shorter fragment (<150 bp) allowed the identification of 76% (n = 68) of 89 previously unidentified blood meals.
source: A trial study based on 89 previously unidentified blood meals using a PCR system amplifying a shorter fragment (<150 bp) (Boessenkool et al., 2012) than the one used in the present study allowed the identification of 76% (n = 68) of the hosts (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a primary data point from the trial study, supported by citation to Boessenkool et al., 2012.

claim: The shorter PCR primers are still not ideal for the purpose as they were designed for optimal amplification of mammal DNA and often fail to properly amplify the DNA of other classes of vertebrates.
source: However, these primers are still not ideal for our purpose as they were designed for optimal amplification of mammal DNA and often fail to properly amplify the DNA of other classes of vertebrates.
evidence: This is an observation about the limitations of the shorter PCR system.

claim: A similar PCR system targeting the entire range of vertebrates still remains to be developed.
source: A similar PCR system targeting the entire range of vertebrates still remains to be developed.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: The trial for amplifying a shorter fragment of Cytb (<200 bp) using a combination of previously published primers did not increase the sensitivity for Plasmodium detection.
source: For Plasmodium, our trial for amplifying a shorter fragment of Cytb (<200 bp) using a combination of previously published primers did not increase the sensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the trial study.

claim: It is possible that other PCR systems, more optimized, could improve the sensitivity of Plasmodium detection.
source: However, it is possible that other PCR systems, more optimized, could indeed improve the sensitivity of Plasmodium detection.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential improvements to the method.

claim: The use of high-throughput sequencing technologies on pools of blood-engorged flies or amplicons could ease the identification of both hosts and parasites.
source: Another direction of improvement could be the use of high-throughput sequencing technologies on pools of blood-engorged flies or amplicons to ease the identification of both hosts and parasites (especially in the case of mixed blood meals or mixed infections).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential improvements to the method.

claim: High-throughput multiplexed pathogen detection methods could be used for the simultaneous testing of many samples in rapid succession.
source: Finally, another way to improve the tool could be to use high-throughput multiplexed pathogen detection methods for the simultaneous testing of many samples in rapid succession.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential improvements to the method.

claim: With improvements, this approach of 'xenorsurveillance' could usefully complete recently developed methods based on the analysis of other invertebrates.
source: With such improvements, this approach of 'xenorsurveillance' could usefully complete recently developed methods based on the analysis of other invertebrates (carrion flies (Hoffmann et al., 2016), mosquitoes [Grubaugh et al., 2015]) and become an innovative way for the concomitant surveillance of many enzootic blood-borne pathogens, such as viruses (chikungunya, Zika), bacteria, protozoa and macro-parasites.
evidence: This is a speculation about the future potential of the method, supported by citations to Hoffmann et al., 2016 and Grubaugh et al., 2015.

claim: The use of hematophagous flies as 'flying syringes' could improve public health management by allowing the surveillance and early detection of zoonotic pathogens.
source: The use of hematophagous flies as 'flying syringes' could indeed improve public health management by allowing the surveillance and early detection of zoonotic pathogens and thus prevent they spread to humans before they cause massive infections.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential public health applications of the method.

claim: This tool could help to better understand the circulation in wildlife of other enzootic viruses, such as chikungunya or Zika.
source: This tool could also help to better understand the circulation in wildlife of other enzootic viruses, such as chikungunya or Zika, especially at the interface between natural/sylvan environments and, consequently, improving our knowledge of their natural history.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of the method.

claim: This method could be useful for monitoring the wildlife diversity within a specific region.
source: From a broader perspective, this method could also be useful for people interested in wildlife biodiversity and conservation. Indeed, it could help monitoring the wildlife diversity within a specific region as demonstrated with other invertebrate systems (Calvignac-Spencer et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2015; Schnell et al., 2012; Schubert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of the method, supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: This method could allow detecting the emergence of new diseases in wild animals that may threaten their long-term survival.
source: More importantly, it could also allow detecting the emergence of new diseases in wild animals that may threaten their long-term survival.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential conservation applications of the method.

claim: Around 60% of emerging diseases in humans are of zoonotic origin.
source: Around 60% of emerging diseases in humans are of zoonotic origin.
evidence: This is a well-established statistic in the field of emerging infectious diseases.

claim: The progressive reduction of wild habitats will increase the contacts between humans and species that are potential reservoirs of diseases.
source: The progressive reduction of wild habitats will increase the contacts between humans and species that are potential reservoirs of diseases.
evidence: This is a prediction based on current trends in habitat loss and disease ecology.

claim: The fly sampling was carried out in four wildlife reserves in Gabon: Moukalaba-Doudou National Park, La Lopé National Park, La Lékédi Park and Ivindo National Park.
source: The fly sampling was carried out in four wildlife reserves in Gabon (Figure 1a): Moukalaba-Doudou National Park (MDNP; S: 2° 26' 08"/E: 10° 25' 18''), La Lopé National Park (LNP; S: 0° 31' 31"/E: 11° 32' 34"), La Lékédi Park (LP; S: 1° 45' 32"/E: 13° 03' 16") and Ivindo National Park (INP; N: 0° 30' 82"/E: 12° 48' 20").
evidence: This is a description of the study sites.

claim: Both MDNP and LNP are dominated by mature forests and mosaic forest-savannah.
source: Both MDNP and LNP are dominated by mature forests and mosaic forest-savannah.
evidence: This is a description of the habitat characteristics of the study sites.

claim: The INP is largely dominated by mature forest with some open biotopes that characterize the secondary forest.
source: The INP is largely dominated by mature forest with some open biotopes that characterize the secondary forest.
evidence: This is a description of the habitat characteristics of the study site.

claim: The LP is a private park dominated by large savannahs and some secondary forest and primary forest patches.
source: The LP is a private park dominated by large savannahs and some secondary forest and primary forest patches.
evidence: This is a description of the habitat characteristics of the study site.

claim: Hematophagous flies were sampled during the rainy and dry seasons between 2012 and 2014.
source: Hematophagous flies were sampled during the rainy and dry seasons between 2012 and 2014.
evidence: This is a description of the sampling timeline.

claim: In INP and MDNP, sampling was done during two years following a gradient of human activity from primary forest to villages.
source: In INP and MDNP, sampling was done during two years following a gradient of human activity from primary forest to villages.
evidence: This is a description of the sampling strategy.

claim: In the other parks, flies were sampled during a single year.
source: In the other parks, flies were sampled during a single year.
evidence: This is a description of the sampling strategy.

claim: Flies were collected by using Vavoua and Nzi traps.
source: Flies were collected by using Vavoua and Nzi traps (Laveissiere and Grebaut, 1990; Acapovi et al., 2001; Mihok, 2002; Gilles et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the sampling method, supported by citations.

claim: The Vavoua trap was initially developed for the capture of tsetse flies and was also successfully used for the capture of stomoxids at La Réunion Island.
source: The Vavoua trap, initially developed for the capture of tsetse flies was also successfully used for the capture of stomoxids at La Réunion Island (Laveissiere and Grebaut, 1990; Gilles et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Laveissiere and Grebaut, 1990 and Gilles et al., 2007.

claim: The Nzi trap was more adapted to the capture of Glossina pallidipes and tabanids in Africa.
source: The Nzi trap was more adapted to the capture of Glossina pallidipes and tabanids in Africa (Acapovi et al., 2001; Mihok, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Acapovi et al., 2001 and Mihok, 2002.

claim: In each park, 24 traps (12 Vavoua and 12 Nzi) were placed during 2 weeks per climatic season.
source: In each park, we placed 24 traps (12 Vavoua and 12 Nzi) during 2 weeks per climatic season.
evidence: This is a description of the sampling design.

claim: Each trap was activated from 7:00 AM to 5:00 PM.
source: Each trap was activated from 7:00 AM to 5:00 PM.
evidence: This is a description of the sampling protocol.

claim: Freshly collected hematophagous flies were identified using a stereo-microscope and taxonomic procedure.
source: Freshly collected hematophagous flies were identified using a stereo-microscope and taxonomic procedure.
evidence: This is a description of the identification method.

claim: The fly species was determined following the determination keys of Pollock (1982), Brunhes et al., 1998, Zumpt, 1973, Garros et al. (2004) and Oldroyd (1973), on the basis of their morphological characteristics.
source: The fly species (tsetse, stomoxids and tabanids) was determined following the determination keys of Pollock (1982), Brunhes et al., 1998, Zumpt, 1973, Garros et al. (2004) and Oldroyd (1973), on the basis of their morphological characteristics, such as size, color, wing venation structure and proboscis.
evidence: This is a description of the identification method, supported by citations to taxonomic keys.

claim: After species identification, engorged flies were dissected individually in a drop of Dulbecco's phosphate buffered saline solution (1x DPBS) to isolate blood meals from midgut.
source: After species identification, engorged flies were dissected individually in a drop of Dulbecco's phosphate buffered saline solution (1x DPBS) to isolate blood meals from midgut.
evidence: This is a description of the dissection protocol.

claim: Each blood meal was transferred in a 1.5-ml microtube containing 50 µl of RNAlater stabilization solution to stabilize and protect nucleic acids.
source: Each blood meal was transferred in a 1.5-ml microtube containing 50 µl of RNAlater stabilization solution (Qiagen: Store at RT Tissue Collection) to stabilize and protect nucleic acids of vertebrate hosts and pathogens contained in the blood meals.
evidence: This is a description of the sample preservation protocol.

claim: Samples were kept at ambient temperature during field session and then frozen at −80°C until DNA extraction.
source: Samples were kept at ambient temperature during field session and then frozen at −80°C until DNA extraction.
evidence: This is a description of the sample storage protocol.

claim: DNA was extracted using the DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer's instructions.
source: Samples were centrifuged at 15,000 rpm at 4°C for 10 min to remove the RNAlater solution. Pellets were used to extract DNA using the DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer's instructions.
evidence: This is a description of the DNA extraction protocol.

claim: Extracted DNA was eluted in 100 µl of buffer AE and stored at −20°C.
source: Extracted DNA was eluted in 100 µl of buffer AE and stored at −20°C.
evidence: This is a description of the DNA storage protocol.

claim: The origin of blood meals was determined using the extracted DNA to amplify a 450 bp fragment of the cytochrome b (Cytb) gene using previously published primers.
source: The origin of blood meals was determined using the extracted DNA to amplify a 450 bp fragment of the cytochrome b (Cytb) gene using previously published primers (Townzen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the blood meal identification method, supported by a citation to Townzen et al., 2008.

claim: When Cytb amplification failed, a 330 bp and/or a 660 bp fragment of the cytochrome oxydase subunit I (COI) gene was amplified using previously described primers and protocols.
source: When Cytb amplification failed, a 330 bp and/or a 660 bp fragment of the cytochrome oxydase subunit I (COI) gene was amplified using previously described primers and protocols (Townzen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the alternative blood meal identification method, supported by a citation to Townzen et al., 2008.

claim: Hosts were identified when the amplified and reference sequences showed at least 98% similarity.
source: Hosts were identified when the amplified and reference sequences showed at least 98% similarity.
evidence: This is a description of the criteria for host identification.

claim: Haemosporidian parasite detection was performed in samples with identified blood meal origin and also in 100 randomly chosen samples for which blood meal origin could not be identified.
source: Haemosporidian parasite detection was performed in samples with identified blood meal origin and also in 100 randomly chosen samples for which blood meal origin could not be identified.
evidence: This is a description of the parasite detection strategy.

claim: Haemosporidian parasites were detected by PCR amplification of a portion of the Cytb gene (~790 bp) using a nested PCR protocol.
source: Haemosporidian parasites were detected by PCR amplification of a portion of the Cytb gene (~790 bp) using a nested PCR protocol, as previously published (Ollomo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the parasite detection method, supported by a citation to Ollomo et al., 2009.

claim: A phylogenetic tree with the haemosporidian sequences obtained in the study and a set of reference sequences was built using Maximum likelihood (ML) methods.
source: A phylogenetic tree with the haemosporidian sequences obtained in our study and a set of reference sequences was built using Maximum likelihood (ML) methods and phylogeny.fr (Dereeper et al., 2008) (see Table 4 for accession numbers).
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis method, supported by a citation to Dereeper et al., 2008.

claim: The ML model used for construction of the tree was GTR (General Time Reversible)+Γ (Gamma distribution)+I (Invariable site distribution).
source: The ML model used for construction of the tree was GTR (General Time Reversible)+Γ (Gamma distribution)+I (Invariable site distribution).
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic analysis parameters.
